column1: What does for_each on a module block actually produce?
column2: One independent module instance per key in the given map — not several copy-pasted module blocks. Each instance has its own full set of internal resources.

column1: How do you address one specific instance of a for_each'd module?
column2: module.<name>[\<key>\"].<output> — e.g. module.tier_sg[\"web\"].id. Referencing it without a key is invalid once for_each is present."

column1: How do you build one combined output covering every instance of a for_each'd module?
column2: A for expression over the module itself: { for k, v in module.tier_sg : k => v.id } — one line instead of a separate output block per key.

column1: Do independent instances of a for_each'd module create in a fixed, sequential order?
column2: No — instances with no dependency on each other create in parallel. Order is only forced when one instance's configuration actually depends on another's output.

column1: What happens to existing for_each'd module instances when you add a new key to the driving map?
column2: Nothing changes for the existing instances — Terraform plans exactly one new resource for the new key, since each instance's identity is tied to its own key, not its position or count.

column1: How does one module's output get passed into a second module's input?
column2: Directly, as a plain reference — e.g. vpc_id = module.vpc.vpc_id inside a second module's call. No manual copying of the value is needed.

column1: Why does this demo scope each tier's security group to the VPC CIDR instead of chaining tier-to-tier?
column2: Chaining (app only accepting traffic specifically from web's security group) is more secure but requires one for_each instance to reference a specific sibling instance's output — a more complex pattern kept separate from the core for_each-on-modules lesson.
